about.title: Inside the Castle
about.length_note: About 32 minutes, a little over the usual 30. There are 37 short beats, one idea each, and 11 check questions. Each part ends on a check, so you can pause between parts. Allow extra time if you sketch your own castle during the final thought experiment.

say.text: Welcome to class 3. Today we go inside a castle. We will see why castles were built, how their parts worked, and who lived there. At the end, you design one.

show.text: Inside the Castle

say.text: One promise first. Real history always comes with sources. Anything from Nimrod's village is invented, and I will say so out loud.

show.text: REAL: castles in the Middle Ages (checked against sources) | INVENTED: Nimrod's castle and the people in it

say.text: Start with the word itself. A castle was a strong medieval building. It was usually the fortified home of a king or a lord.

show.text: Castle = a fortified home of a king or lord

ask.q: Which sentence best describes a medieval castle?
ask.right: A strong building that was usually the fortified home of a king or lord.
wrong: A market square with a low fence around it.
A church built only for prayer.
A tent camp for an army on the move.
ask.why: A castle was a fort and a home in one. Britannica describes it as the fortified dwelling of the king or lord of the area.

say.text: Job one was defence. In England, early castles were mostly forts. They helped the Normans guard land they had just conquered.

show.text: Job 1: defence

say.text: Here is a word you will need. A siege is when an army surrounds a place and tries to break in. Defence mostly means surviving a siege.

show.text: Siege = an army surrounds a place and tries to take it

say.text: Job two was running things. Once the Normans were settled, a castle could be a centre for local government, administration and justice.

show.text: Job 2: government, administration, justice

say.text: Job three was being a home. A 1396 record from Portchester Castle lists new building work: a hall, a kitchen, chambers and offices.

show.text: Hall | Kitchen | Chambers | Offices

ask.q: Besides defence, which job could a medieval castle do?
ask.right: Act as a centre for local government, administration and justice.
wrong: Print books for the whole kingdom.
Grow all the food for every village.
Run a ferry across the sea.
ask.why: The National Archives says castles could serve as centres of local government, administration and justice. The Portchester record shows homes and offices being built inside.

say.text: Now the defences. Picture layers, like an onion: moat, wall, gate, keep. We take them one at a time, from the outside in.

show.text: 1 Moat | 2 Curtain wall | 3 Gate | 4 Keep

say.text: First, the moat. It is a ditch around a castle. It was usually, but not always, filled with water.

show.text: Moat = a ditch around the castle

say.text: Why dig one? Once castles had stone walls, a moat kept moving towers and battering rams away from the walls until attackers filled the ditch.

show.text: Attackers pushing a tall wooden tower toward a wall, stopped at the edge of a wide ditch

ask.q: What did a moat do for the defenders?
ask.right: It kept siege towers and battering rams from reaching the walls until the ditch was filled.
wrong: It let the castle be seen from far away.
It gave attackers a quick way inside.
It let defenders shoot arrows farther.
ask.why: Britannica explains that the moat blocked moving towers and rams from reaching the walls until it was filled.

say.text: Next, the curtain wall. It is the wall that joins the towers together and circles the castle.

show.text: Curtain wall = a wall connecting towers

say.text: The top of the wall was built for fighting. It had battlements to shelter behind. Defenders could shoot from behind cover, and a wall walk let them move along the top.

show.text: A stone wall seen from the side, with a walkway along the top and notched battlements

ask.q: What was the wall walk for?
ask.right: Defenders could fight from it or move along the top of the wall.
wrong: Merchants sold goods on it.
It was where the moat was dug.
It was the king's bedroom.
ask.why: The wall walk sat behind the battlements. Defenders used it to fight or to move between parts of the castle.

say.text: Now the gate, and here is the puzzle. A castle needs a way in. People and supplies must pass in peacetime. But in a siege, that entrance is the most vulnerable point.

show.text: One way in: the part attackers want most

say.text: The fix was the gatehouse. Builders packed it with obstacles, and the weakest spot became one of the strongest.

show.text: Gatehouse = the entrance, heavily defended

say.text: A drawbridge could be lifted. A portcullis, an iron-covered wooden grill, slid down in front of the door. Beams could be slid behind the doors to hold them shut.

show.text: Drawbridge | Portcullis (sliding grill) | Wooden beams behind the doors

say.text: Inside, the passage was a trap. A lowered gate could catch attackers there. Murder holes in the roof let defenders drop things like hot sand or scalding water on them.

show.text: A narrow stone passage with a grill at each end, and openings in the roof above

ask.q: Why did builders put so many defences at the gate?
ask.right: The entrance was the most vulnerable point, so they made it strong.
wrong: Gates were the only part made of stone.
Attackers never went near the gate.
It was cheaper than building walls.
ask.why: A castle needed an entrance, and that made it the weak point in a siege. Builders answered with a heavily defended gatehouse.

say.text: At the centre was the keep. It was the strongest part of the castle, the place of last resort if the rest fell. It could be a single tower or a larger fortified enclosure.

show.text: Keep = the last place to fall back to

say.text: Put it together, outside in. A moat surrounded the outer wall. A heavily protected gateway led in. Walled courtyards, called baileys, surrounded the keep.

show.text: A bird's-eye plan: a ring of water, then a wall with one gate, then courtyards, then a tower in the middle

ask.q: In a siege, which part was the place of last resort?
wrong: The moat
The wall walk
The drawbridge
ask.why: The keep was the strongest part of the castle and the final place to fall back to.

say.text: Castles did not stay the same. Here is the story in four steps. We will take each one in turn.

show.text: 10th-11th centuries: wood and earth (motte and bailey) | then: stone replaces wood | late 12th-13th centuries: concentric castles | 15th-16th centuries: firearms end the age

say.text: First came the motte and bailey. The motte was a mound topped by a wooden tower. The bailey was a defended yard beside it.

show.text: A grassy mound with a wooden tower on top, and a fenced yard alongside

say.text: Often the wooden defences were later replaced in stone. At Totnes Castle, for example, stone took the place of wood.

show.text: Wood, then stone

say.text: Then came concentric castles. They had two rings of towered walls, one inside the other. Attackers had to take them section by section, and then face a second set of defences.

show.text: A castle plan with a low outer wall ringing a taller inner wall, towers on both

ask.q: What made a concentric castle so hard to attack?
ask.right: It had two rings of towered walls, one inside the other.
wrong: It was built on a single mound of earth.
It had no gate at all.
It was made only of wood.
ask.why: English Heritage describes two mutually supporting rings of towered walls. Attackers had to break through one ring and then another.

say.text: What ended the castle age? Firearms. As they spread in the 15th and 16th centuries, the age of the medieval castle came to an end.

show.text: Firearms ended the castle age

ask.q: What ended the age of the medieval castle?
wrong: Moats drying up everywhere.
Kings giving away all their land.
Walls becoming too thin to build.
ask.why: Britannica says the medieval castle age ended with the increasing use of firearms in the 15th and 16th centuries.

say.text: Now the people. First, the lord. In the usual classroom picture, a king granted pieces of land, called fiefs, to nobles. These were lords or barons, and they owed loyalty and service in return.

show.text: Lord = a noble who held land

say.text: Now the knight. A king could also grant land to knights in exchange for military service. Many knights were professional warriors in a lord's army. In return the lord gave them lodging, food, armour, weapons, horses and money.

show.text: Knight = a mounted warrior who served

say.text: Knights were not only fighters. In peacetime they often managed estates. They oversaw repairs, handled money, inspected goods and food, and made sure rent and taxes were collected.

show.text: Repairs | Money | Checking goods and food | Collecting rent and taxes

say.text: So the difference is this. A lord held land and ruled it. A knight served a lord, mostly as a warrior and manager. The lines could overlap, because an estate might be owned by a lord or a knight.

show.text: LORD: holds land, rules it, often lives in a castle | KNIGHT: serves a lord or the king, fights, often manages an estate

ask.q: What is the main difference between a lord and a knight?
ask.right: A lord held land and ruled it; a knight served a lord or the king, mainly as a mounted warrior.
wrong: Lords fought in battle and knights never did.
Knights owned all the castles and lords lived in villages.
There was no difference; they were the same word.
ask.why: Lords held land granted by the king. Knights served in a lord's army and often ran estates in peacetime.

say.text: A fair warning. This is the tidy classroom version. Some historians argue that the neat picture of fiefs and vassals is too simple. See the other side notes for more.

show.text: A tidy picture?

say.text: Now we leave history and make things up. INVENTED: King Kenny and Queen Rose rule from a castle above Nimrod's village. Like real castles, it is a home, an office and a fort.

show.text: INVENTED: Nimrod's castle

say.text: INVENTED: Sir Michael is the castle's defender. Like a real knight, he serves his king. His job is to keep the walls, the gate and the people safe.

show.text: Sir Michael: defender (invented)

say.text: INVENTED: Princess Jess and Prince Vince grow up here. To them it is simply home, with a hall, a kitchen and rooms of their own. Nimrod the cat patrols the wall walk, as cats do.

show.text: Two children in a stone hall by a fire, with a cat sitting on a high window ledge

say.text: Time for the thought experiment. Robin the Joker says: build the castle with no door, then nobody can get in! Ha. Why would that fail?

show.text: Thought experiment: where do you put the weak point?

say.text: Because people and supplies must get in and out in peacetime. So every castle has a way in. Real builders could not remove the weak point. They chose where it was and how strong to make it.

show.text: You cannot remove the weak point. You can choose it.

ask.q: Why can a castle not simply have no entrance?
ask.right: People and supplies need to get in and out in peacetime.
wrong: Doors were against the law.
Walls were too thick to build around a door.
Kings preferred to climb in with ladders.
ask.why: Exploring Castles says the entrance was essential in peacetime, even though it was the most vulnerable point during a siege.

say.text: Here is your brief. Design a simple castle for King Kenny and Queen Rose. Decide each part below, and above all, decide where the gate goes and why.

show.text: 1 Moat: yes or no? | 2 Curtain wall and towers | 3 The gate: WHERE, and why? | 4 The keep | 5 Homes for Kenny, Rose, Jess and Vince | 6 An office where Kenny holds court | 7 Sir Michael's wall walk

say.text: One possible answer, in the story. Put the gate on the side facing the village road. Add a drawbridge, a portcullis at each end of a long passage, and holes in the roof. If attackers get in, they are trapped, and Sir Michael's archers wait.

show.text: A gate on the village side: a drawbridge over the moat, then a passage with a grill at each end and archers above

say.text: Your turn. Sketch your castle and mark the weak point. Then check your thinking with this question. There is more than one good design.

show.text: Your turn: sketch it, mark the weak point

ask.q: Which gate design best follows the idea 'put the weak point where it is hardest to attack'?
ask.right: A gate behind a drawbridge, at the end of a passage with two portcullises, covered by archers.
wrong: A gate in the middle of a flat wall with no towers.
A gate with no door, so it can never break.
Two gates side by side with nobody guarding them.
ask.why: The real gatehouse turned the weak point into a trap. It had a drawbridge, portcullises and defenders able to fire down into the passage.

say.text: Let us finish with the big ideas. A castle was a fort, an office and a home. Its moat, wall, gate and keep worked as layers. Designs changed over time. A lord held land, and a knight served.

show.text: Fort, office and home | Layers: moat, wall, gate, keep | Wood to stone to concentric | Lord holds land, knight serves | Choose your weak point

say.text: Next class, we leave the castle for the sky. We will look at where dragons come from, and the real myths behind them. Well done today.

show.text: Next: Where Dragons Come From

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Motte-and-bailey castles appeared in continental Europe, between the Rhine and Loire rivers, and later spread across most of western Europe. In England, a chronicler noted that Normans' castles were scarcely known there before them.
In Japan, Himeji Castle was rebuilt and expanded in these years. A fort had first stood on its hill in 1333. Meanwhile, in western Europe, firearms had already ended the age of the medieval castle.

other_side.claim: Castles were built mainly to defend against attack.
other_side.other_view: Some historians since the 1990s argue that late medieval castles were built mainly to show status. At Bodiam Castle (1385) they point to features such as an easy-to-drain moat, thin walls and badly placed gunports. Others say Bodiam had a real military purpose. Some scholars now say the 'defence versus status' argument is too simple, and that Bodiam changed across several periods.

other_side.claim: In the Middle Ages, lords gave land (fiefs) to knights (vassals) in exchange for service.
other_side.other_view: This is the traditional textbook picture. Historian Susan Reynolds argued in 1994 that the ideas of fiefs and vassalage rest on a misreading of the medieval sources. Historians still discuss whether 'feudalism' is a useful label, so treat the lord-and-knight chart as a simplified model.
